title: Football lawmakers plan punishment for players covering mouths when speaking to opponents
content:
Any player who covers their mouth when speaking to an opponent is set to be punished after football’s lawmakers confirmed their intention to bring in new measures ahead of the World Cup.

A consultation around a new law being introduced comes less than a fortnight after Benfica’s Gianluca Prestianni was alleged to have racially abused Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior during a Champions League play-off tie in Lisbon.

Prestianni, 20, covered his mouth with his shirt when addressing the Brazil international, making it unclear what was said. A UEFA investigation remains ongoing, with the Argentine winger denying that he used racist language, but the International Football Association Board (IFAB) will move to deter further incidents of that nature.

IFAB’s annual general meeting, held in Wales on February 28, covered the issue and an agreement was reached to develop measures that would punish players who cover their mouths when confronting opponents.

“Clearly there are circumstances we want to prevent,” Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the English Football Association and IFAB board member, told reporters in a press conference that followed the AGM.

“We need to consult the game more broadly and work out where we would avoid any unforeseen circumstances. You can see when a player is talking to an opponent, there are very few circumstances where they should need to cover their mouth when they are confronting them.

“We need to look at everything and make sure if we were going to bring in a rule change or a penalty for that, that we’re not going to create further problems. There’s a process we’ll go through but there’s a desire to bring something in relatively quickly.”

FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafstrom added the potential to see new punishments introduced ahead of the World Cup beginning in June.

“We want to continue the discussion and potentially come up with measures before the World Cup,” he said. “We will have the FIFA Congress in Vancouver (on April 30), everybody will be there, and that will be an opportunity to have a discussion.”

It is not yet clear if covering the mouth will be an offence punishable by a yellow or red card, but tackling the issue is unlikely to be straightforward. Players can often be seen shielding their mouths with a cupped hand when interacting with teammates, coaching staff, and even opponents, to hide what is being said from cameras.

Prestianni went a step further when pulling his shirt up to below his nose when speaking to Vinicius Jr. The incident that brought a lengthy stoppage in the first leg of Real Madrid’s eventual victory over Benfica on February 17.

Pierluigi Collina, chairman of the FIFA Referees Committee and part of IFAB’s technical subcommittee, added: “If it had been easy, probably the decision would’ve been different. We would not have the need to explore or find how to deal with this, which is what was decided today.

“We all understand this is an issue, something that should not occur in a football match. We have to find the best way to solve this problem.”
